 Section 1: A Spring Alone Versus a Mass-Spring System

   A spring stops at a place, but a mass stops after a process. This single idea separates two
     very different kinds of motion. A spring with no mass attached returns to one location
    and stays there. A spring with a mass attached keeps moving past that location, back and
      forth, before it finally comes to rest.
         Everything here is measured with one number, the displacement x .
         Displacement is how far the end of the spring is from its natural position, the
          place where the spring rests when nothing is pulling or pushing on it. We call
          the natural position x = 0 , a stretch to the right x = +1 , and a squeeze to the
             left x = −1 .

    The spring alone, pulled out. Picture a spring fixed to a wall at one end, lying on a table,
     with nothing attached to its free end. If we pull the free end out to x = +1 and let go, the
     spring pulls itself back and stops exactly at x = 0 . It does not overshoot.
       When we plot x against time for this release, the curve starts at +1 and bends
         downward, dropping quickly at first and then more and more slowly. The curve
          gets closer and closer to 0 but never crosses below it. The label for this motion is
         "x approaches 0 without crossing it."

        The reason the motion slows down is that the pull of the spring depends on how
           far it is stretched. A large stretch produces a large pull back, and a small stretch
         produces a small pull. As the end gets close to x = 0 , the pull becomes almost
           zero, so the motion becomes almost zero too.

    The spring alone, pushed in. The same thing happens in the opposite direction. If we
     squeeze the spring to x = −1 and release it, the spring pushes itself back out and settles
      at x = 0 .
          Plotted against time, this curve starts at −1 and rises toward 0 , again quickly at
             first and then more slowly. It flattens out right at 0 and never goes above it. The
           label is "x rises toward 0 without crossing it."
        Whether we start from +1 or −1 , a massless spring always ends at the same
          place and never passes through it. That is what it means to say a spring stops at
         a place.

    Adding a mass changes the behavior completely. Now a mass, drawn as a small cart on
     wheels, is attached to the free end of the spring. We pull the mass to x = +1 and release
        it. The mass does not stop at x = 0 . It shoots right through the natural position and keeps
     going to the other side.

        The mass keeps going because a moving mass carries its motion with it. When
          the mass reaches x = 0 , the spring is no longer pulling on it, but the mass is
          already moving fast, so it continues past 0 and compresses the spring on the
          other side.

        Once the spring is compressed, it pushes the mass back. The mass slows down,
          stops briefly near x = −1 , and then gets pushed back through x = 0 toward
          the positive side again. The label for this is "the mass carries motion through
         every crossing."
          Plotted against time, x now makes a wave. It starts at +1 , falls through 0 to
          nearly −1 , rises back through 0 to nearly +1 , and repeats. This repeating back-
          and-forth motion is called oscillation.

     Lightly damped oscillation. Each swing of the mass is slightly smaller than the one
     before it, so the peaks of the wave shrink a little over time. This is called a lightly damped
      oscillation. Damping is anything that slowly drains away the motion, such as friction.
    With light damping, the mass swings many times before it finally settles at x = 0 .

          This is why a mass stops after a process. It does eventually come to rest at the
          natural position, but only after a long sequence of crossings back and forth,
         each one a little smaller than the last.

      A mass-spring system therefore has a frequency, which is the number of back-
          and-forth cycles it completes per second. A massless spring has no frequency at

all, because it never swings.


Section 2: Perturbation Theory

    Perturbation theory asks what happens to the behavior of a system when we change one
    of its properties. To perturb a system means to nudge one of its settings. For a mass-
    spring system, the two settings that matter are the mass m and the stiffness k of the
    spring, and the behavior we care about is the frequency f of the oscillation.

    Increasing the mass decreases the frequency. If we attach a heavier mass to the same
    spring, it oscillates more slowly, so the frequency goes down.

      A heavier mass is harder to speed up and harder to slow down. The spring pulls
       on it with the same strength as before, but that pull changes the heavier mass's
        speed less. Each swing takes longer, so fewer swings fit into one second.
         In short form: when m goes up, f goes down.

    Increasing the stiffness increases the frequency. If we keep the same mass but use a
     stiffer spring, the oscillation speeds up, so the frequency goes up.
         Stiffness k is how strongly a spring resists being stretched or squeezed. A
           stiffer spring pulls back harder for the same amount of stretch. That stronger
          pull speeds the mass up faster, so each swing finishes sooner and more swings
             fit into one second.
         In short form: when k goes up, f goes up.

    These two rules together are the core of perturbation theory for oscillators. More mass
   means lower frequency, and more stiffness means higher frequency. We do not need to
    calculate an exact frequency to use these rules. We only need to know which direction the
    frequency moves when mass or stiffness changes.


Section 3: Speech as Changing Mass and Stiffness of Air

   Speaking changes the effective mass and stiffness of air in the vocal tract. The vocal
    tract is the air-filled tube running from the vocal folds in the throat up through the
   mouth to the lips. When we speak, we move the tongue, jaw, and lips, and these
   movements squeeze some portions of the air in that tube and open up others.

        Squeezing a portion of air in one place changes how much that air acts like a
       mass and how much it acts like a spring. The effective mass and effective
          stiffness of each portion of air are different for every vowel and every
         consonant, because each sound uses a different shape of the tube.

       The air in the vocal tract is set into vibration by the vibration of the vocal folds.
        Because the tube has different mass and stiffness in different places, the air
         vibrates at many frequencies at once. The particular set of frequencies
        depends on where the air is squeezed and how much it is squeezed, so each
        vowel and consonant has its own set.

   MRI images of five vowels make these shapes visible. Each image is a side view of the
   head sliced down the middle, taken while a speaker says one word. The bright, rounded
   mass in the middle of each image is the tongue, and the dark regions are the air spaces of
    the mouth and throat. The five words are dean, dune, done, Dan, and Don, which differ
    only in their vowel.

         In dean, the tongue is pushed high and forward, almost filling the front of the
       mouth right up under the roof of the mouth. This leaves a wide dark air space in
         the throat behind the tongue. The air is squeezed tightly at the front and left
        open at the back.

         In dune, the tongue is also high but is bunched toward the back of the mouth,
        and the lips are pushed forward. The narrow squeeze is further back than in
          "dean," with an open air space in front of the tongue.

         In done, the tongue sits in a middle position, neither very high nor very low, and
         neither far forward nor far back. The air space above the tongue is moderate in
           size.

         In Dan, the jaw is lower and the tongue is lower and toward the front, leaving a
          large air space in the mouth above the tongue.

         In Don, the jaw is open widest and the tongue is low and pulled back toward the
          throat. The air space in the mouth is large, while the air in the throat behind the
        tongue is squeezed.

        Each of these five tongue positions squeezes the air in a different place and by a
          different amount. By perturbation theory, each shape gives the air a different
        combination of mass and stiffness in different regions, and therefore a different

set of vibration frequencies. That set of frequencies is what makes "dean" sound
          different from "Don."

   The listener has to recover these frequencies from the sound. For a listener to
    understand speech, the ear has to figure out which low, middle, and high frequencies are
    present in the speaker's voice and how strong each one is. The brain then has to use that
    information to decide which sound was spoken.

         For example, hearing a high frequency of one particular strength together with
        a low frequency of another particular strength might tell the brain that the
        word was "scene." Hearing two other frequencies instead might tell the brain
         that the word was "son."

       The question is how the ear separates a single incoming sound into its separate
         frequencies and reports each one to the brain. The answer lies in the structure
          of the inner ear.


Section 4: How We Hear and the Cochlea

   Sound is a wave of vibration in the air. When someone speaks, waves of vibration travel
    through the air and arrive at the listener's external ear, the part of the ear on the outside
    of the head. From there, the vibration travels inward through the ear canal toward the
    inner ear.

   The cochlea is the part of the inner ear that reports frequencies to the brain. Of all the
    structures in the ear, the cochlea is the essential one to know by name. It is a small, coiled
    tube shaped like a snail shell, buried deep inside the bone of the skull. The cochlea is the
    part that sends signals to the brain saying which frequencies are present in a sound.

   The inner ear and its parts. In a cutaway view of the head, the outer ear and ear canal
    lead inward to a tiny structure boxed off deep in the skull, and that boxed region is the
    inner ear. Enlarged, the inner ear has two main regions.

       The upper region contains three looping tubes called the semicircular ducts,
       named anterior, lateral, and posterior, along with two small sacs called the
          utricle and saccule. Small sensory structures called cristae sit inside swellings
          at the base of the loops, called ampullae. These structures are part of the same
         inner ear but are not the part that separates sound frequencies.

       The lower region is the coiled cochlea. Running through the cochlea are three
           fluid-filled channels lying side by side: the vestibular duct, the cochlear duct,
        and the tympanic duct. These channels spiral together around the coil.

       The inner ear is built as a set of soft, membrane-walled tubes, called the
       membranous labyrinth, sitting inside a matching set of hollow spaces in hard
         bone, called the bony labyrinth. The soft inner tubes are where the sensing
        happens, and the bone around them protects them.

      A bundle of nerve fibers called the vestibulocochlear nerve leaves the inner
         ear and runs toward the brain. This nerve carries the cochlea's signals about
        sound frequencies to the brain.


Section 5: The Basilar Membrane

   Sound reaches the cochlea through a chain of structures. Sound waves in the air first
    strike the tympanic membrane, which is the eardrum. The tympanic membrane is a thin
    sheet stretched across the end of the ear canal, and it vibrates back and forth as the air
    pressure pushes on it.

       The tympanic membrane is attached to the first of three tiny bones, the
         malleus. When the eardrum vibrates, it moves the malleus.

       The malleus is connected to the second bone, the incus, so the malleus's
         vibration moves the incus.

       The incus is connected to the third bone, the stapes. The stapes sits against an
        opening in the cochlea, so when the stapes vibrates, it pushes in and out on the
          fluid inside the cochlea.

         This chain carries the vibration from the air outside, through the eardrum and
         three small bones, into the fluid of the inner ear.

   The basilar membrane runs the length of the cochlea. Inside the coiled cochlea is a
    long, thin strip of tissue called the basilar membrane. It begins near the stapes, where
    vibration enters the cochlea, and it follows the spiral all the way to the tip of the coil at the
    center.

       The opening at the very tip of the coil is called the helicotrema. The basilar
       membrane extends from the stapes end of the cochlea all the way in to the
         helicotrema.

When the stapes pushes on the cochlear fluid, the fluid moves, and that
       movement makes the basilar membrane vibrate. The basilar membrane is the
         structure that turns the vibration of the fluid into information about frequency.


Section 6: How the Basilar Membrane Separates Frequencies

   The basilar membrane is not the same all along its length. If we imagine uncoiling the
    cochlea and laying the basilar membrane out flat as a long strip, one end of the strip is
   wide and the other end is narrow. The wide end is the part near the helicotrema, and the
    narrow end is the part near the stapes.
        At the wide end, the membrane has a large mass, labeled M , and a small
          stiffness, labeled k . This end is heavy and floppy.
        At the narrow end, the membrane has a small mass, labeled m , and a large
          stiffness, labeled K . This end is light and stiff.

        Between the two ends, the mass gradually decreases and the stiffness gradually
         increases along the length of the membrane.

   Each spot on the membrane acts like its own mass-spring system. Every small piece of
    the basilar membrane has its own mass and its own stiffness, so every piece has its own
    natural frequency of vibration. Perturbation theory tells us which way that frequency
    goes along the membrane.

        At the heavy, floppy end, large mass lowers the frequency and small stiffness
          also lowers the frequency. Both effects push in the same direction, so this end
         vibrates at low frequencies.

        At the light, stiff end, small mass raises the frequency and large stiffness also
          raises the frequency. Both effects again push in the same direction, so this end
         vibrates at high frequencies.

         Therefore frequency increases steadily along the membrane, from low
         frequencies at the heavy, floppy end to high frequencies at the light, stiff end.

  A sound with many frequencies is sorted out by place. When a sound containing
    several frequencies at once enters the cochlea, each frequency makes the part of the
   membrane tuned to that frequency vibrate the most. A low-frequency component shakes
    the heavy, floppy region, and a high-frequency component shakes the light, stiff region.

      A single complex sound, such as a vowel, is thus spread out along the
        membrane, with each of its frequencies causing strong vibration at its own
          location. How strongly each location vibrates reflects how strong that
        frequency is in the sound.

   Neurons along the membrane report the pattern to the brain. Rows of neurons are
    attached along the length of the basilar membrane. When a region of the membrane
    vibrates, the neurons attached to that region send signals, and those signals travel to the
    brain.

       The brain can tell which frequencies are present by noticing which neurons are
          active, since each neuron is connected to a location that responds to one
          particular frequency. It can tell how strong each frequency is by how strongly
         those neurons are signaling.

         This is how the listener's brain can register "a high frequency of this much and a
        low frequency of this much." A pattern of activity at one set of locations
         corresponds to "scene," and a pattern at a different set of locations corresponds
          to "son."

   Georg von Békésy won the Nobel Prize in 1961 for his work on how the cochlea
    responds to sound. His work established that different frequencies cause the strongest
    vibration at different places along the basilar membrane, which is the mechanism that
     lets the ear separate a sound into its frequencies.

Section 7: Vocal Folds

   The vocal folds are two small muscles in the throat. Each vocal fold is about 1 cm in
    length and about 1 mm in height. The folds sit across the airway, and air from the lungs
    has to pass between them on its way up to the mouth.

         In a camera view looking down the throat at the vocal folds during speech, the
        two folds meet along a line, and the gap between them appears as a narrow dark
             slit. That slit is the opening that air passes through, and it is the space that
         repeatedly opens and closes when the folds vibrate.

Muscle has mass and stiffness, so the vocal folds behave like a mass-spring system.
    Since a vocal fold has both mass and stiffness, it can oscillate just like the mass on a
    spring, and perturbation theory applies to it directly.

        About 10 other muscles are attached to the bones and cartilages of the
         structure that houses the vocal folds. By pulling on that housing, these muscles
        can change the vocal folds in two ways.

       They can stretch the folds, which makes them stiffer. By perturbation theory,
         greater stiffness raises the frequency of vibration.

       They can bunch the folds together, which makes them effectively heavier. By
         perturbation theory, greater mass lowers the frequency of vibration.

         In this way, speakers control how fast their vocal folds vibrate by adjusting their
          effective mass and stiffness.

    Controlling vocal fold frequency serves several purposes. Speakers change this
    frequency constantly, and it carries different kinds of information in different settings.

         In singing, changing the vibration frequency of the vocal folds is how a singer
        produces different musical notes.

         In English, changes in this frequency convey questions, mistrust, degree of
          belief, surprise, emotion, and more. The same words can mean different things
        depending on how the frequency rises and falls across them.

         In a tone language, changes in this frequency distinguish the meanings of
        words. Two words with identical consonants and vowels can be completely
          different words if they are spoken with different vocal fold frequencies.

    Pitch, F0, and fundamental frequency. The vibration frequency of the vocal folds is
    called pitch. It is also called F ​0, which stands for the fundamental frequency. A higher
   F ​0 means the vocal folds are opening and closing more times per second, and listeners
    hear this as a higher pitch.


Section 8: How the Vocal Folds Vibrate

    Air pressure from the lungs blows the vocal folds apart. When we take air into our lungs
   and then close the vocal folds, the air cannot escape, so a lot of pressure builds up
    beneath the folds. If that pressure becomes high enough, it forces the vocal folds apart,
   and air begins to flow up through the gap between them.

   The flowing air sucks the vocal folds back together. Air rushing through the narrow gap
   between the folds pulls the folds back inward toward each other. This works just like a
    curtain in a shower, which gets pulled inward toward the running water.

       The inward pulling force created by fast-moving air is called the Bernoulli
          force. The same force is what lifts airplanes.

       Once the Bernoulli force pulls the folds back together, the gap closes and the
          airflow stops.

   The cycle repeats hundreds of times per second. With the folds closed again, pressure
    builds beneath them once more, and it blows them apart again. The airflow then sucks
   them back together, and the pressure blows them apart yet again.

       1. Pressure builds beneath the closed vocal folds.

       2. The pressure becomes high enough to blow the folds apart, and air flows
        between them.

       3. The Bernoulli force from the flowing air sucks the folds back together, closing
         the gap.

       4. With the gap closed, pressure builds again, and the cycle starts over.

         This cycle repeats hundreds of times per second. Each full cycle of opening
        and closing is one vibration, so the number of cycles per second is the
        fundamental frequency F ​0. The mass and stiffness of the folds, set by the
        surrounding muscles, determine how fast this cycle runs.

Section 1: A Spring Alone Versus a Mass-Spring System

  A spring stops at a place, but a mass stops after a process. A spring with no mass
    attached returns to one location and stays there. A spring with a mass attached keeps
   moving past that location, back and forth, before it finally comes to rest.
        Motion is measured with the displacement x , which is how far the end of the
         spring is from its natural position. The natural position is where the spring
          rests when nothing pulls or pushes on it, and it is called x = 0 . A stretch is
       x = +1 , and a squeeze is x = −1 .

  A spring alone never crosses its natural position. A spring fixed to a wall with nothing
   on its free end, when pulled to x = +1 and released, pulls itself back and stops at x = 0 .
   Over time, x drops quickly at first and then more and more slowly, getting closer to 0
    without ever crossing it.
       The motion slows down as the spring nears x = 0 , since the spring's pull
        depends on how far it is stretched. A large stretch produces a large pull back,
        and a small stretch produces a small pull, so near x = 0 the pull is almost zero.
      When the spring is squeezed to x = −1 and released, the same thing happens
          in the opposite direction. x rises toward 0 , quickly at first and then slowly, and
        never goes above it.
        Whether it starts at +1 or −1 , a massless spring always ends at the same place
         without passing through it. This is what it means for a spring to stop at a place.

  A mass on the spring keeps moving through the natural position. When a mass is
    attached to the spring, pulled to x = +1 , and released, it does not stop at x = 0 . It passes

right through the natural position and keeps going to the other side.
       The mass carries its motion with it. When it reaches x = 0 , the spring is no
         longer pulling on it, but the mass is already moving fast, so it continues past 0
        and compresses the spring.

       The compressed spring pushes the mass back. The mass slows, stops briefly
        near x = −1 , and is pushed back through x = 0 toward the positive side. The
       mass carries its motion through every crossing.
        Over time, x forms a wave. It starts at +1 , falls through 0 to nearly −1 , rises
        back through 0 to nearly +1 , and repeats. This repeating back-and-forth
        motion is called oscillation.

    Lightly damped oscillation. Each swing of the mass is slightly smaller than the one
    before, so the peaks of the wave shrink a little over time. This is a lightly damped
     oscillation, meaning the motion is slowly drained away but the mass still swings many
    times before settling.
       The mass therefore stops after a process. It eventually rests at x = 0 , but only
          after a long series of crossings, each a little smaller than the last.

      A mass-spring system has a frequency, the number of back-and-forth cycles it
        completes per second. A spring alone has no frequency, since it never swings.


Section 2: Perturbation Theory

    Perturbation theory asks which direction a system's behavior changes when one of its
    properties is changed. For a mass-spring system, the two properties are the mass m and
    the stiffness k , and the behavior is the frequency f of the oscillation.

    Increasing the mass decreases the frequency. A heavier mass on the same spring
     oscillates more slowly.

      A heavier mass is harder to speed up and harder to slow down. The spring's pull
        changes its speed less, so each swing takes longer and fewer swings fit into one
         second. When m goes up, f goes down.

    Increasing the stiffness increases the frequency. The same mass on a stiffer spring
     oscillates faster.
         Stiffness k is how strongly a spring resists being stretched or squeezed. A
           stiffer spring pulls back harder for the same stretch, so it speeds the mass up
           faster, each swing finishes sooner, and more swings fit into one second. When k
        goes up, f goes up.

    Together, these rules are the core of perturbation theory for oscillators: more mass
   means lower frequency, and more stiffness means higher frequency. No exact
    frequency needs to be calculated to use these rules, only the direction of the change.


Section 3: Speech as Changing Mass and Stiffness of Air

   Speaking changes the effective mass and stiffness of air in the vocal tract. The vocal
    tract is the air-filled tube from the vocal folds in the throat, through the mouth, to the lips.
   Moving the tongue, jaw, and lips squeezes some portions of that air and opens up others.

        Squeezing a portion of air changes how much it acts like a mass and how much
              it acts like a spring. The effective mass and effective stiffness of each portion
          of air are different for every vowel and every consonant, since each sound gives
         the tube a different shape.

         Vocal fold vibration sets the air in the vocal tract vibrating. Since the air has
          different mass and stiffness in different places, it vibrates at many frequencies
          at once. This set of frequencies depends on where the air is squeezed and how
       much, so each vowel and consonant has its own set.

   Each vowel squeezes the air in a different place. In side-view MRI slices through the
    middle of the head, the tongue appears as a bright rounded mass and the air spaces of the
   mouth and throat appear dark. The words dean, dune, done, Dan, and Don differ only in
    their vowel, and each vowel has a different tongue position.

         In dean, the tongue is high and forward, almost filling the front of the mouth
        under its roof, with a wide air space in the throat behind the tongue. The air is
        squeezed at the front and open at the back.

         In dune, the tongue is high but bunched toward the back of the mouth, and the
           lips are pushed forward. The squeeze is further back than in "dean," with open
           air space in front of the tongue.

         In done, the tongue sits in a middle position, neither very high nor very low and
         neither far forward nor far back.

In Dan, the jaw and tongue are lower, with the tongue toward the front, leaving
        a large air space above the tongue.

         In Don, the jaw is open widest and the tongue is low and pulled back, leaving a
          large air space in the mouth while squeezing the air in the throat behind the
         tongue.

       By perturbation theory, each tongue position gives the air a different
        combination of mass and stiffness in different regions, and therefore a different
          set of vibration frequencies. That set of frequencies distinguishes one vowel
        from another.

   The listener must recover these frequencies. To understand speech, the ear has to
    determine which low, middle, and high frequencies are in the speaker's voice and how
    strong each is. The brain then uses that information to decide what was said.

         For example, a high frequency of one strength combined with a low frequency
          of another strength may signal the word "scene," while two other frequencies
          signal the word "son." The ear must separate one incoming sound into its
         individual frequencies and report each to the brain.


Section 4: How We Hear and the Cochlea

   Sound is a wave of vibration in the air. Waves of vibration from a speaker travel through
    the air, arrive at the listener's external ear, and travel inward to the inner ear.

   The cochlea sends frequency information to the brain. The cochlea is the part of the
    inner ear that sends signals to the brain saying which frequencies are present in a sound.
     It is the one anatomical name in the ear that is essential to know. The cochlea is a small
    coiled tube, shaped like a snail shell, deep within the skull.

   The inner ear has two main regions. The inner ear sits deep in the skull, inward from the
    external ear and ear canal.

       The upper region contains three looping semicircular ducts, named anterior,
           lateral, and posterior, along with two sacs called the utricle and saccule.
         Structures called cristae sit within swellings at the bases of the loops, called
        ampullae.

       The lower region is the coiled cochlea. Three channels run side by side through
              it and spiral together around the coil: the vestibular duct, the cochlear duct,
        and the tympanic duct.

       The inner ear consists of soft membrane-walled tubes, the membranous
         labyrinth, sitting inside matching hollow spaces in bone, the bony labyrinth.

       The vestibulocochlear nerve leaves the inner ear and runs toward the brain,
         carrying the cochlea's signals.


Section 5: The Basilar Membrane

    Vibration reaches the cochlea through a chain of structures. Sound waves first strike
    the tympanic membrane, the eardrum, which vibrates as the air pressure pushes on it.

       The tympanic membrane is attached to the first of three tiny bones, the
         malleus, so its vibration moves the malleus.

       The malleus is connected to the second bone, the incus, and moves it.

       The incus is connected to the third bone, the stapes. The stapes sits against the
         cochlea, so its vibration is passed into the cochlea.

   The basilar membrane runs along the cochlea. Inside the coiled cochlea is a long, thin
     strip of tissue called the basilar membrane. It begins near the stapes, where vibration
    enters, and follows the spiral to the center of the coil, where the helicotrema is located.

         Vibration passed in by the stapes makes the basilar membrane vibrate. The
          basilar membrane is the structure that turns this vibration into information
        about frequency.


Section 6: How the Basilar Membrane Separates Frequencies

   The basilar membrane changes in mass and stiffness along its length. When the
    basilar membrane is uncoiled and laid out flat as a strip, one end is wide and the other end
     is narrow.
       The wide end has a large mass M and a small stiffness k , so it is heavy and
          floppy.
       The narrow end has a small mass m and a large stiffness K , so it is light and
             stiff.

Between the two ends, mass gradually decreases and stiffness gradually
          increases.

   Each spot on the membrane acts as its own mass-spring system. Each small piece of
    the basilar membrane has its own mass and stiffness, so each piece has its own frequency
    of vibration. Perturbation theory sets the direction of that frequency along the
   membrane.

        At the heavy, floppy end, large mass lowers the frequency and small stiffness
          also lowers it. Both effects work together, so this end vibrates at low
         frequencies.

        At the light, stiff end, small mass raises the frequency and large stiffness also
          raises it. Both effects work together, so this end vibrates at high frequencies.

        Frequency increases steadily along the membrane, from the heavy, floppy
        end to the light, stiff end.

  A sound with many frequencies is sorted by place. When a sound containing several
    frequencies enters the cochlea, each frequency makes the part of the membrane matched
    to that frequency vibrate most. Low-frequency parts of the sound shake the heavy, floppy
    region, and high-frequency parts shake the light, stiff region.

      A single complex sound, such as a vowel, is spread out along the membrane,
        with each of its frequencies producing strong vibration at its own location. How
         strongly each location vibrates reflects how strong that frequency is in the
         sound.

   Neurons along the membrane carry the pattern to the brain. Neurons are attached
    along the length of the basilar membrane. When a region vibrates, the neurons attached
    to it send signals to the brain.

       The brain identifies which frequencies are present by which neurons are active,
         since each neuron is attached to a location that responds to a particular
         frequency. It identifies how strong each frequency is by how strongly those
        neurons signal.

         In this way the brain registers "a high frequency of this much and a low
        frequency of this much." One pattern of activity along the membrane
         corresponds to "scene," and a different pattern corresponds to "son."

   Georg von Békésy won the Nobel Prize in 1961 for explaining how hearing works in this
    way.


Section 7: Vocal Folds

   The vocal folds are small muscles. Each vocal fold is about 1 cm in length and 1 mm in
    height. The two folds sit across the airway, and during speech the gap between them is a
    narrow slit that air passes through.

   Muscle has mass and stiffness, so the vocal folds oscillate like a mass-spring system.
    Perturbation theory applies to them directly.

        About 10 other muscles are attached to the bones and cartilages of the housing
          of the vocal folds. These muscles change the folds in two ways.

       They can stretch the folds, making them stiffer, which raises the frequency of
          vibration.

       They can bunch the folds, making them effectively heavier, which lowers the
        frequency of vibration.

   Changing vocal fold frequency serves several purposes.

         In singing, it produces different notes.

         In English, it conveys questions, mistrust, degree of belief, surprise, emotion,
        and more.

         In a tone language, it distinguishes the meanings of words.
    Pitch, F ​0, and fundamental frequency. The vibration frequency of the vocal folds is
    called pitch, also written F ​0, the fundamental frequency. A higher F ​0 means the folds
   open and close more times per second.


Section 8: How the Vocal Folds Vibrate

    Air pressure blows the vocal folds apart. When we take air into the lungs and close the
    vocal folds, a lot of pressure builds beneath them. If the pressure is high enough, it blows
    the folds apart, and air flows between them.

   The airflow sucks the vocal folds back together. Just like a curtain in a shower, the
    flowing air sucks the vocal folds back inward. This suction force is called the Bernoulli
    force, the same force that lifts airplanes.

Once the folds are pulled together, the airflow stops, and pressure builds
        beneath them again. The pressure blows them apart again, the airflow sucks
       them back in again, and the cycle repeats hundreds of times per second.

        Each opening and closing is one vibration, so the number of cycles per second is
      F ​0. The mass and stiffness of the folds, set by the surrounding muscles,
        determine how fast this cycle runs.

Section 12: Solving Differential Equations with Arithmetic, Python, and Software 1.0

Euler's explicit method solves differential equations using arithmetic. A differential
                                                                            kequation is an equation about rates of change, such as x˙ = v and v˙ = −  ​x . The                                             m
method, named for Leonhard Euler, turns each one into an update of the form x[n] =
… dt + x[n −1] , in which the new value is the previous value plus a rate times a small
time step.

    Each update uses only multiplication and addition. Repeating these arithmetic
     steps follows the motion of a system, such as a mass on a spring, through time.
    Work done with arithmetic methods of this kind has been honored with a
    medal at a formal ceremony.

The Euler steps are carried out in Python. A Python loop repeats the arithmetic for as
many steps as needed, computing one new position and one new velocity on each pass
and appending them to lists.

Software 1.0 is software in which people write out every instruction the computer
follows, step by step. The Euler loops are an example, since every arithmetic operation is
spelled out by the programmer.

     Large Software 1.0 programs filled stacks of printed code as tall as the person
    who wrote them, and that hand-written software was honored with a medal
     presented at a presidential ceremony.
